messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Roofer
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Maladaptive Strategies: Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Assertiveness: never disagree or assert myself to avoid conflict, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Hopelessness: I have no future, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 66, Minh Tran had spent most of his adult life roofing in southern Louisiana, proud of being the man who could stay steady high above the ground in punishing heat and get a crew through a long day. The event that broke that sense of himself happened on a commercial job at dusk, when he and two younger workers were finishing near an industrial site and a release of toxic fumes drifted across the roof. He remembered the sharp chemical smell first, then the sudden burning in his throat and eyes, the panic of trying to breathe while the light dropped and everything around him seemed to turn unreal. He was taken to the hospital overnight for observation, and the antiseptic odor in the emergency department mixed in his mind with the same choking fear. What has stayed with him is not only the exposure itself but the particular combination of darkness, chemical smell, and hospital disinfectant; waking in a dark room or catching a similar smell can make it feel as if he is back in those first minutes when he thought his body was failing him.

In the months after, those moments began arriving with little warning. If he woke before dawn and opened his eyes into a dark bedroom, or if he passed a clinic and caught the hospital-clean smell, a memory would begin “like a film,” as he described it, replaying the roof, the fumes, the scramble for air in vivid detail. At other times there was no picture at all, only the same crushing dread and bodily alarm, as if the emotional force of the event had surged forward on its own. These experiences left him on edge long after the trigger had passed. He found that even when he knew he was at home and objectively safe, he could not relax; his attention narrowed and he had trouble concentrating on simple tasks, following a conversation, or estimating measurements at work. Unfamiliar places became especially difficult because he felt he could not judge what hidden danger might be there.

Minh had come to believe something fundamental had changed in him. Before the exposure he thought of himself as dependable, practical, the one others leaned on. Now he was increasingly certain he could not rely on himself, and that conviction sharpened everything around him. He watched the world as if danger were always close, and because he saw it as a dangerous place, the dark, strange smells, and medical odors stood out immediately to him wherever he went. The future also felt closed off. He spoke bleakly about having no future worth planning for, less in a dramatic way than with a tired certainty that life had narrowed to getting through each day without something going wrong.

Those conclusions shaped how he managed himself. Convinced he was no longer someone who could trust his own judgment, he tried to avoid making waves anywhere: at home with his wife, with supervisors, with the younger men on the crew. If a job site felt unsafe or a smell bothered him, he often said nothing, fearing conflict and doubting he would handle it well. He also worked hard to push the trauma out of his mind. When the memories started or when he felt that wave of fear without an image, he would clamp down and try not to think about it, or he would drift into dwelling on the man he used to be before the incident—stronger, clearer, less afraid. But the more he tried to force the memory away, the more readily a smell or waking in darkness seemed to catch him off guard, and the more those cues governed his day.

The cycle had tightened over time. Because he stayed tense and scanned for danger, he noticed possible triggers quickly, and once he noticed them the old film returned more easily. After a bad spell he would spend hours comparing himself to his former self, and by the end of it he felt even less capable and more hopeless. On roofing jobs this had become concrete: in unfamiliar neighborhoods or on new commercial sites, he struggled to focus and silently waited for someone else to decide what to do, which embarrassed him and fed his sense that he could not rely on himself. At home he avoided disagreeing with anyone, especially his wife, and she had begun to experience him as distant and withdrawn rather than simply quiet.

By the time he sought help, Minh was sleeping lightly and dreading the moment of waking in the dark because he expected fear before he was fully conscious. He was alarmed by how quickly a disinfectant smell at a medical office, or even a vaguely chemical odor on a job, could pull him back. What frightened him most was the thought that this was now permanent—that the world would remain dangerous, that he would keep shrinking his life to stay ahead of the next trigger, and that the capable man he had been before the exposure was gone for good. He came to treatment hoping, cautiously, that he might learn how to live without being ruled by darkness, smell, and the certainty that he can no longer trust himself.
